    session DO re-checks user status. Pinned by an integration test (code
    exchange + refresh expires_in, KV expiration, TTL < idle window).

-- Idle-based expiry for MCP logins ("sliding session"), replacing the
-- library's absolute refresh-token lifetime.
--
-- `workers-oauth-provider` stamps `grant.expiresAt = authorized_at +
-- refreshTokenTTL` ONCE, at the authorization-code exchange, and never slides
-- it: the refresh path re-saves the same absolute `expiration`, and the
-- token-exchange callback is explicitly forbidden from changing
-- `refreshTokenTTL`. A client that refreshed perfectly every hour was still
-- logged out on a fixed date — the 30 d default, then our 90 d (migration-era
-- `MCP_LOGIN_TTL_SECONDS`). The DCR client record had the same shape
-- (`clientRegistrationTTL`, stamped at registration, never renewed on use),
-- so it capped the login independently.
--
-- Both TTLs are now passed as `undefined` — the KV records carry no
-- expiration at all — and the expiry policy lives here instead: a grant dies
-- when it has not been REFRESHED for `MCP_LOGIN_IDLE_DAYS`. Refreshing keeps
-- you signed in; going quiet logs you out.
--
-- One row per live grant. `last_refresh_at` is stamped by the provider's
-- `tokenExchangeCallback` on every exchange (code + refresh); the nightly
-- `grant-idle-prune` job reconciles this table against KV and revokes the
-- rows that went quiet (oauth/grant-sweep.ts).
--
-- No FK to `users`: KV is authoritative for grants and this table is a stamp
-- ledger the sweep reconciles against it (seeding missing rows, deleting
-- orphans), so a NOT NULL child of `users` would only add a parent-rebuild
-- landmine (conventions §G1) for integrity the sweep already provides.
CREATE TABLE oauth_grant_activity (
  grant_id        TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         TEXT NOT NULL,
  client_id       TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  last_refresh_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);

-- The sweep's read: oldest-quiet first.
CREATE INDEX idx_grant_activity_idle ON oauth_grant_activity(last_refresh_at);
-- Per-user cleanup (suspend/delete revokes every grant a user holds).
CREATE INDEX idx_grant_activity_user ON oauth_grant_activity(user_id);

I'm stopping here without the query result. The prod D1 read was blocked last session, so this one is for you to run. The logs alone don't settle it.

**What the logs show**

| Time (UTC) | Client | Event |
|---|---|---|
| until 19:01 Nov 8 | — | worker `2e32d87b` (the 1-hour access tokens) |
| 19:24 Nov 8 → | — | worker `4f852b7b` (the 7-day tokens, deploy `5e07c18`) |
| all night | hosted connector (`python-httpx`) | every refresh request (246-byte body) succeeds; no `invalid_grant` |
| 06:19:38 | hosted connector | refresh succeeds |
| **06:20:14** | hosted connector | **fresh sign-in (450-byte body = authorization-code exchange) — almost certainly yours** |
| 20:30:10 Nov 8 | hosted connector | one sign-in returned 400, the retry 18 s later succeeded |
| 19:31–19:32 Nov 8 | a Portuguese client | two 401s, then 200 on retry; not you |

Claude Code (`Bun`, your Gent IP) last refreshed at 19:32, right after the deploy, and hasn't needed to since. That fits a 7-day token, though it's weak evidence.

**The server didn't reject you.** Nothing the server does on the MCP path assumes 1-hour tokens. The session-epoch check only applies to the web app's cookie, and the credential-freshness check only gates upstream tool calls. No refresh failed. So the hosted connector chose to start a full sign-in itself.

**Which of two cases it is depends on when your old connector login last refreshed:**
- **Before ~19:07 Nov 8:** it was still holding a 1-hour token. This is the one extra prompt per client I predicted last session, and from here prompts should drop to about once a week.
- **After 19:07:** it already had a 7-day token and still sent you to sign in. Then a longer token isn't enough, and the connector is throwing away a working login. That would be worth adding to anthropics/claude-ai-mcp#1237.

**Query to tell them apart** (read-only, your own rows, prints no tokens):

```
! cd ~/Projects/satisa/ctxlayer && wrangler d1 execute DB --remote -c wrangler.yukitools.toml --command "SELECT a.grant_id, a.client_id, datetime(a.created_at,'unixepoch') created, datetime(a.last_refresh_at,'unixepoch') last_refresh FROM oauth_grant_activity a JOIN users u ON u.id=a.user_id WHERE u.email='stevenn@satisa.be' ORDER BY a.last_refresh_at DESC"
```

You should see a login created around 06:20 today, plus the older hosted-connector login it replaced. That older row's `last_refresh` timestamp decides the case. One more useful detail: did you get a full browser sign-in this morning, or just a Reconnect click?
it was a full browser sign-in, not a Reconnect
it was a full browser sign-in, not a Reconnect - in the Claude Desktop client

A full browser sign-in matters, because it's different from yesterday's pattern. Then, the Reconnect click quietly reused your existing login: it swapped the refresh token for a new access token. This morning Desktop went straight to a brand-new sign-in instead. That's consistent with the logs: no refresh attempt failed, so Desktop either never tried its refresh token or ignored a successful one. The 06:19:38 refresh, 36 s before your sign-in, may have been yours.

So the server didn't log you out. Desktop dropped or skipped a login that still worked. What I still can't tell without the query is whether that login held an old 1-hour token or a new 7-day one:

| Old connector login's last refresh | Meaning |
|---|---|
| before ~19:07 Nov 8 | Its 1-hour token expired overnight. On that 401 Desktop sometimes does a full sign-in rather than a refresh. The 7-day tokens should make this rare from now on, about once a week at most. |
| after 19:07 Nov 8 | It held a valid 7-day token and Desktop still sent you to the browser. A longer token won't fix that, and it should go into anthropics/claude-ai-mcp#1237 as a second symptom. |

Same query as before, read-only, your own rows, prints no tokens:

```
! cd ~/Projects/satisa/ctxlayer && wrangler d1 execute DB --remote -c wrangler.yukitools.toml --command "SELECT a.grant_id, a.client_id, datetime(a.created_at,'unixepoch') created, datetime(a.last_refresh_at,'unixepoch') last_refresh FROM oauth_grant_activity a JOIN users u ON u.id=a.user_id WHERE u.email='stevenn@satisa.be' ORDER BY a.last_refresh_at DESC"
```

You should see a new row created around 06:20 today. Look for an older row with the same `client_id`: its `last_refresh` decides which case this is. If there's no older row with that `client_id`, Desktop registered itself as a new client and threw away its whole earlier registration, which also belongs in the issue.

**Resolved — the root cause was on our side (Microsoft Entra ID), not the client.**

Closing the loop, because this thread ended on the assumption that the client wasn't requesting `offline_access`. That assumption was wrong, and the real cause is likely to bite anyone running an MCP server behind Entra ID.

### Following the suggestion in this thread

We pointed `authorization_endpoint` at our own host and injected `offline_access` before redirecting to Entra. Two things came out of that:

1. The authorization request arriving at our shim **already contained** `offline_access openid profile`, plus `prompt=consent`. The client was requesting it on its own — our injection was a no-op. (We kept the shim as a guarantee, not as a fix.)
2. The connector still died at every access-token expiry.

### Instrumenting the token endpoint

`token_endpoint` still pointed straight at Microsoft, so the code→token exchange never passed through us and we had no way to see whether a refresh token was ever issued. We proxied it through our own host, logging metadata only — grant type, whether a refresh token came back, `expires_in`, scope. Never tokens or secrets.

That answered the first question immediately:

```
canje OK: grant_type=authorization_code refresh_token=SI expires_in=4150
```

Entra *was* issuing a refresh token.

(Log lines below are ours and in Spanish: `canje` = exchange, `SI`/`NO` = yes/no.)

The second question needed a different method. Waiting passively for the connector to die produces only silence in the logs, and silence is ambiguous — an idle client that never refreshes looks exactly like one that would refresh if it had work to do. So we forced demand: invoked a tool *after* the access token had expired. That produced:

```
canje FALLIDO: grant_type=refresh_token status=400 error=invalid_request
desc=AADSTS90009: Application '<client-id>'(<client-id>) is requesting a
token for itself. This scenario is supported only if resource is
specified using the GUID based App Identifier.
```

**The client does attempt the refresh.** Entra was rejecting it.

### The actual cause

Microsoft's error message is misleading. It uses v1.0 terminology (`resource`, "GUID based App Identifier") and reads as though the resource identifier is wrong. On the v2.0 endpoint the real cause is that the refresh request carries no resource scope — only the reserved OIDC scopes (`openid profile offline_access`). With no resource to target, Entra falls back to the degenerate "the app is requesting a token for itself" case, and reports the consequence rather than the cause.

Corroborated by [AzureAD/microsoft-authentication-library-for-js#5198](https://github.com/AzureAD/microsoft-authentication-library-for-js/issues/5198) (reproduced in Postman: changing the scope to the API's own scope turns the 400 into a 200) and by the Microsoft Q&A thread ["Confusing error message on failed refresh token request"](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/192699/confusing-error-message-on-failed-refresh-token-re) — `scope` is documented as optional but is required once custom scopes are involved.

### Fix

In our token proxy, for `grant_type=refresh_token` only, we append the API scope and `offline_access` to whatever scope the client sent. `authorization_code` exchanges pass through byte-for-byte untouched — that exchange never failed, and we didn't want to risk it.

`offline_access` matters on the refresh as well: Entra rotates refresh tokens, so omitting it would return a renewed access token with no successor, trading a failure every hour for a failure every two.

### Verified in production

Two consecutive expiry cycles, both survived without any manual reconnection:

```
canje OK: grant_type=authorization_code refresh_token=SI expires_in=3887 scope_inyectado=NO
canje OK: grant_type=refresh_token      refresh_token=SI expires_in=5292 scope_inyectado=SI
```

The first cycle was tested 2 minutes after the access token expired; the second, 85 minutes after. In both cases a tool call returned normal results with no reconnection, no prompt, and no user intervention.

`scope_inyectado` is a flag we added deliberately so a success couldn't be misattributed: it records whether our injection actually did anything. `NO` on the `authorization_code` exchange is correct — that path is untouched. `SI` on the refresh confirms the fix is what unblocked it, rather than some unrelated change.

The second cycle mattered independently: the first only proved *that* refresh worked, not that the successor token would. Chaining two proves the mechanism sustains itself.

Since then the connector has run for a full day of normal use — roughly 15–20 chained renewals, all silent, with no reconnection at any point.

### What this means for the client

Nothing to fix regarding refresh — Claude's client behaves correctly, and our earlier report mischaracterized it. Apologies for the noise on that point.

One part of the original report does still stand, and it's the reason this took weeks rather than an afternoon: when the refresh fails, the connector surfaces "connection was invalidated" only when a tool is invoked, while the UI keeps showing it as connected. The provider returned a specific, actionable error every single time — it just never reached anyone who could act on it. Surfacing the identity provider's error at the moment the refresh fails would turn this class of problem from a multi-week forensic exercise into a one-line diagnosis.

### For anyone else behind Entra ID

If your MCP connector dies at every access-token expiry, check whether your refresh requests carry your API's scope. `AADSTS90009` will point you at the wrong thing.

Connector never requests offline_access (no refresh token); connection silently dies at token expiry and shows as connected
CLOSED
**Summary:** Claude never requests `offline_access`, so no refresh token is ever issued. When the access token expires (~1h for Microsoft Entra ID), the connector silently stops working: the UI still shows it as connected, tool calls fail, and the only recovery is a manual disconnect/reconnect. Both documented mechanisms for influencing the requested scopes are implemented on our server and verifiable from the public internet; neither takes effect.

This is a separate issue from #786 (which was about `code_challenge_methods_supported` and is resolved) — same server, same deployment, next problem down the chain.

## Setup

Self-hosted remote MCP server (Python SDK `mcp` 1.29.0, `FastMCP`, Streamable HTTP), added as a Custom Connector with pre-registered OAuth Client ID + Secret. Authorization server is Microsoft Entra ID (single-tenant); the MCP server is a pure resource server (validates bearer tokens, never issues them).

## What our server advertises — both verifiable right now with curl

**1. `scope` parameter in the `WWW-Authenticate` header of the 401**, per [Authentication for connectors](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/authentication): *"To control which scopes Claude requests, include a `scope` parameter in the `WWW-Authenticate` header on your `401` response."*

```
$ curl -si -X POST https://mcp.fidechile.com/mcp -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
    -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}' | grep -i www-authenticate

www-authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Authentication required",
  resource_metadata="https://mcp.fidechile.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp",
  scope="https://mcp.fidechile.com/mcp/access_as_user offline_access openid profile"
```

**2. `offline_access` in the authorization server metadata's `scopes_supported`**, per the same page: *"Claude also appends `offline_access` when your authorization server metadata lists it in `scopes_supported`, to obtain a refresh token."*

```
$ curl -s https://mcp.fidechile.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/entra-facade | jq .scopes_supported
[
  "https://mcp.fidechile.com/mcp/access_as_user",
  "openid",
  "profile",
  "offline_access"
]
```

## Observed behavior

Neither mechanism results in `offline_access` being requested:

- **Entra ID's permission grants are empty.** Enterprise applications → (our app) → Permissions shows zero entries under both *Admin consent* and *User consent*, after multiple successful connections. If `offline_access` had been requested and granted, a delegated permission grant would exist.
- **No consent prompt is ever shown** on connect (the user has an active M365 session, so authorization completes via silent SSO — Entra sign-in logs confirm: client app `Browser`, MFA `Previously satisfied`, latency 111 ms).
- **Reproducible expiry failure.** Leave the connector idle for ~2 hours, then invoke any tool. Result, client-side:

  > The user's connection to this connector was invalidated. The user needs to reconnect it.

  Server-side journal for a matching earlier occurrence:

  ```
  Aug 12 11:32:56  GET https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/discovery/v2.0/keys → 200
  Aug 12 11:32:56  Token rejected (ExpiredSignatureError): Signature has expired
  Aug 12 11:32:56  POST /mcp → 401
  ```
  followed by **78 minutes of complete silence** — zero requests of any kind from Anthropic's range — until the user manually reconnected, at which point a full fresh discovery sequence appears (`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` → AS metadata → JWKS → new transport → ListTools). Recovery never happens without manual intervention.

The docs state Claude *"refreshes tokens reactively on a 401 response, with a proactive refresh up to five minutes before the stored expiry."* With no refresh token available, no refresh is possible — and rather than surfacing an auth error, the connector goes quiet while continuing to display as connected.

## Impact

Any MCP server using Microsoft Entra ID as its authorization server is unusable beyond the access-token lifetime (1 hour by default) without a manual reconnect every session. For our engineering team this means reconnecting the connector each morning, and again after any pause longer than an hour.

That comment is a good find, but its cause can't be ours. Their MCP server passed token requests straight through to Microsoft Entra, so Entra handled every refresh and rejected them (with the misleading `AADSTS90009` error). ctxlayer issues and refreshes its own tokens. Entra, or whichever sign-in provider is used, only appears when you sign in through the browser. In your logs every refresh against our token endpoint returned 200, so there's no hidden rejection like theirs.

Two of their points do carry over:

1. **No log lines doesn't prove the client never tried.** An idle client looks just like one that wouldn't refresh if it had work to do. That applies to us. With a token issued at 20:17 and valid for 7 days, Desktop had no reason to refresh overnight, so "no refresh attempt" in my posted comment is weaker evidence than it reads. The new client registration and full sign-in while it held a valid token still stand.
2. **Force the moment instead of waiting for it.** I only looked at the token endpoint. I never checked what Desktop sent to `/mcp` just before 06:20. If it called `/mcp` with its 7-day token and got a 401, that would be our bug, not Desktop's. My code check found nothing in our code that answers 401 on `/mcp`; only the OAuth library does, for an invalid or expired token. But I haven't confirmed it from the logs.

**To close that gap:** in Workers Logs, filter to path `/mcp` (and `/sse`), Anthropic addresses `160.79.106.*`, between **06:10 and 06:21 UTC today**, and paste the status codes. With other users on the gateway, look at the requests around 06:19–06:20.

| What you see | Meaning |
|---|---|
| A 401 on `/mcp` just before 06:20 | Our server rejected a valid token. That's a bug to chase on our side, and I'd add a correction to #1237. |
| No `/mcp` traffic before the sign-in | Desktop dropped the login without even trying it. The posted comment stands. |

If the logs don't settle it, their method gives us a clean test: in the Desktop chat that's connected now, call a tool, leave it idle for a few hours, then call a tool again and watch for a 401 and for which token request follows.

No case of our server rejecting a valid token. Your posted comment stands.

**What happened at 06:20, from the `/mcp` log:**

| UTC | Request | Status | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 06:20:07.4 | `POST /mcp` from `python-httpx` with **no `Authorization` header** | 401 | Desktop's backend had no token for this connector at all. A request without credentials gets a 401, and that's what starts the sign-in flow. |
| 06:20:14 | new sign-in exchanged for tokens (`/oauth/token`, seen earlier) | 200 | your browser sign-in |
| 06:20:15 | `server/discover`, protocol `2026-07-28` | 400 | the new connection's first request, see below |
| 06:20:21 → | `initialize` / `tools/list` / tool calls | 200 | connected |

Across the whole 06:10–06:22 window there's not a single 401 on a request that carried a token. Desktop didn't try the old token and get refused; it came back with no credentials at all. That matches the new-client-every-time pattern in the login table.

Two side findings, neither of them the cause:

1. **`server/discover` → 400.** Some Anthropic clients now try protocol version `2026-07-28` with a `server/discover` call first (4× in this window). Our server rejects it, and the client falls back to the older `initialize` (protocol `2025-11-25`), which works. It's harmless today, but it's a sign of a newer protocol version we don't support yet. Worth a look before clients stop falling back.
2. **Slow handshakes.** `initialize` takes 15.0–15.7 s nearly every time, and `notifications/initialized` and `tools/list` take about 10 s. The suspiciously constant 15 s looks like a fixed timeout somewhere on the connect path, possibly a hung upstream. Tool calls running 10–35 s could just be the upstreams being slow. Users feel the handshake time though.

I'd leave #1237 alone; the logs back it up. Want me to dig into the 15-second `initialize` next, or into what `server/discover` needs?

To tell server time apart from the Workers wall clock I need our own per-call latency numbers. `wallTimeMs` also counts background work that keeps running after the response has gone out. Notice `notifications/initialized` answered 202 yet "took" 10 s, while the same request in another session finished in 0.5 s. This read pulls the recorded latencies for the same window. Read-only; no user IDs or message content:

```
! (set -a; . ~/Projects/satisa/ctxlayer-ops/.tenant-secrets/yukitools-cf.env; set +a; curl -sS --max-time 30 -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/a94cb5880b72350ddbc9b930b374e83c/d1/database/7ffed976-a02d-4dfe-80d8-8b4b22556d44/query" -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"sql":"SELECT ts, substr(session_id,1,8) sess, tool, latency_ms, status FROM usage_events WHERE (ts BETWEEN 1794204600 AND 1794205400) OR (ts BETWEEN 1794204600000 AND 1794205400000) ORDER BY ts"}' > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-stevenn-Projects-satisa-ctxlayer/890cbf3d-0d8f-461c-98e0-541c8f7b3ad3/scratchpad/latency.json 2>&1; echo "exit=$?" >> /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-stevenn-Projects-satisa-ctxlayer/890cbf3d-0d8f-461c-98e0-541c8f7b3ad3/scratchpad/latency.json)
```

**What I've found so far**

- **`server/discover`:** this is the next MCP protocol revision (`2026-07-28`). Under it, servers must answer a `server/discover` call listing their supported versions and capabilities. content.text:
The 15-second requests aren't a real slowdown, and neither finding needs work now.

**The 15 s requests.** Cloudflare's log time also counts work the worker keeps doing after it has sent the response. Our own per-call timings show the server answering fast:

| Tool | Our server's time (56 calls) | Cloudflare log time |
|---|---|---|
| `list_upstreams` | 39–216 ms | 14–30 s |
| `get_skill` | 315–638 ms | 9–28 s |
| `up-driver__grep_source` | 274–742 ms | 12–35 s |
| `up-sentry__search_issues` | ~4.9 s (Sentry itself) | 19–32 s |

So each request carries a 10–15 s tail after the response has gone out. Clients aren't waiting for it: the hosted connector fires its next call within a second or two. `initialize` isn't recorded in our timings because it isn't a tool call. It shows the same 10–15 s tail, so it's very likely fast too, but I haven't measured it. The only slow item is Sentry, at about 5 s, and that time is spent on Sentry's side.

The tail itself is probably the response connection, or the library's cleanup after it, staying open for a while. It's worth knowing about only if it shows up as cost. I wouldn't change anything for it.

**`server/discover`.** This call belongs to the next MCP protocol version (`2026-07-28`). Our server is built on MCP SDK 1.30, which stops at `2025-11-25`. When Anthropic's clients try the new version first, they get a 400 and fall back to the older handshake, which works. Supporting it properly means moving our session layer to the v2 SDK, which is a large change. I'd hold off until the `agents` library ships a v2-based server class, or until a client stops falling back.

I've added both findings to my notes, including that the Cloudflare log time shouldn't be read as response time in future debugging.

The tail is harmless. The Worker stays alive after the response has been sent, so clients don't wait for it, and on your plan Workers bill CPU time, not wall time.

**How `/mcp` works.** `McpAgent.serve` in the `agents` library (`agents/dist/mcp/index.js`) doesn't handle a POST in the Worker. It opens an internal WebSocket to the session's Durable Object and passes the message through. The answer streams back to the client, and when it's complete the Worker closes the stream and the WebSocket. For a notification it's even simpler: it closes the WebSocket and returns 202 straight away. Yet those 202s also show 10 s in the logs. So the extra time comes after the response is sent, while the Worker waits for the internal WebSocket to finish closing.

**The evidence.** I worked out each request's start time by subtracting its duration from the log timestamp, and lined that up with our own recorded tool timings:

| Session | Request (log time) | Started | Our tool timing | Work done by | Log entry ends | Tail |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| e7b3… | `list_upstreams` (06:15:05.330) | 06:14:50.7 | 199 ms | ~06:14:51.0 | 06:15:05.3 | ~14 s |
| 758d… | `get_detailed_changelog` (06:17:03.193) | 06:16:46.6 | 2.2 s | ~06:16:50 | 06:17:03.2 | ~13 s |

The wait before each tool started was at most about 1.5 s; all the extra time is at the end. Many requests also finish in groups at exactly the same millisecond: four at 06:18:41.207, four at 06:18:00.200, four at 06:20:55.127. Those requests started seconds apart, so something shared releases them all together. My best guess is that the close acknowledgements from the session object arrive in batches, but I haven't pinned down what triggers the release.

**What it costs**

| | Impact |
|---|---|
| Client response time | none; the response has already been delivered |
| Workers billing | none; CPU is 1–16 ms per request and wall time isn't billed |
| Durable Object billing | probably none; the session objects go idle between calls (noted in an earlier session), but I haven't confirmed that against billing |
| Observability | `wallTimeMs` on `/mcp` doesn't tell you response time; use our own tool timings instead |

**Recommendation:** leave it. It lives in the `agents` library's request relay, not our code. The only real fix is changing how that library relays requests, or building our own `/mcp` entry point, and neither is worth it for something that doesn't affect users or cost. If you want, I can draft a short issue for `cloudflare/agents` with the grouped end times as evidence.

# @cloudflare/agents

## 0.33.0

This release adds support for [Pi 1.5](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.5.0/packages/durable/CHANGELOG.md#150---2026-11-02), which makes `PiHarness` much faster and lighter on memory, and lets you continue a run that ended without an answer.

### Highlights

- **Pi 1.5 support:** `agents/harness/pi`, `agents/models/pi-ai` and the Pi tools now run on Pi 1.5.
- **Far fewer storage writes while streaming:** Pi stores streamed answers and tool output in batches, at the latest every second, instead of on every update. Over SQLite this cuts storage transactions about 27x for long answers and 5.7x for turns with parallel tools, and CPU by about a quarter. A crash can now lose up to about a second of streamed output.
- **Faster with many sessions:** Pi's scheduler no longer rechecks every conversation on each commit, so on SQLite one Pi harness with 2,048 sessions went from 88 to 459 agent runs per second. Commits that arrive together now share one storage call, and a normal run makes no storage reads.
- **Large answers no longer blow up memory:** streaming a 500 KB tool call used to take about 20 s of CPU and a 100 MB heap, and a 140 KB answer followed by a 140 KB tool call held over 100 MB. Pi now appends new text instead of copying it on every update.
- **Conversation view:** `session.watch()` replaces `session.events()`. It returns the newest transcript entries and the session's live state, such as the answer being streamed, running tools, and why the last run ended without an answer. `session.entries()` pages older entries. See [Work with sessions](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/harnesses/pi.md#work-with-sessions).
- **Continue a run:** `session.continue()` starts a run on the transcript as it is, without a new message, for example after the model errored or the run hit its turn limit.
- **Turn limit:** `defaults.maxTurns` caps the tool rounds a run can take in new sessions. A run that reaches it ends without an answer, with reason `turn_limit`.
- **Crash-looping tasks end instead of parking:** a tool call cut off by Pi's restart limit ends with an error result the model sees, and a model request ends its run without an answer, with reason `restart_limit`. See [How recovery works](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/harnesses/pi.md#how-recovery-works).
- **Other changes:** `submit()` takes `whenIdle: "reject"`, so an idle session refuses input instead of starting a run. Streamed tool-call arguments on the chat-completions wire that aren't valid JSON now fail the tool call with an error the model can fix. In Pi's code mode, `browserTool` gives scripts its run as an object, with screenshots as image blocks for `image()`. `browserTool` stops when the harness aborts its call, and `BrowserSession` lets code outside `browserTool` run the same `browser` object. `useAgentChat().stop()` now cancels server-started turns streamed without a resume handshake.

### Upgrading

You only need to make changes if you use the Pi harness, `agents/models/pi-ai` or the Pi tools.

1. **Update Pi to `~1.5.0`** (`@earendil-works/pi-durable`, `pi-ai`, `chord`) and install `@earendil-works/pi-schema` alongside them. Once a conversation runs on Pi 1.5, Pi 1.4 cannot read it, so a deployment cannot roll back past this release. Roll forward to fix a bad deploy instead.
2. **Check [pi-durable's 1.5.0 changelog](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.5.0/packages/durable/CHANGELOG.md#150---2026-11-02)** for its breaking changes, such as the removal of `watchEvents()`, tagged watch calls and ends, and `ConversationView.entries` becoming a window over the transcript.
3. **Replace `session.events()` with `session.watch()`** and render the view each time it changes. To show a transcript longer than the window, merge each value into Pi's `ConversationTranscript`, which pages older entries with `session.entries()`. The view's entries now include those before a reset or compaction: Pi adds the reset or summary in place instead of cutting the transcript there. An idle `pi.live` now keeps `runFailure` after a failed run, so check `run === undefined` instead of comparing it with `{}`.

   ```diff
   - const stream = await session.events();
   - initialize(stream.snapshot);
   - stream.start(async (events) => events.forEach(apply));
   + const watch = await session.watch();
   + render(watch.value);
   + watch.start(async (call) => {
   +   if (call.kind === "value") render(call.value);
   + });
   ```

4. **Build your Pi tool schemas with `@earendil-works/pi-schema`**, as pi-ai no longer exports TypeBox's `Type`. Unlike `Type.Object`, `obj()` rejects properties it doesn't list; pass `{ open: true }` to allow them. To keep TypeBox instead, import `Type` from `typebox`.

   ```diff
   - import { Type } from "@earendil-works/pi-ai";
   - const WordCount = Type.Object({ text: Type.String() });
   + import { obj, str } from "@earendil-works/pi-schema";
   + const WordCount = obj({ text: str() });
   ```

5. **Remove calls to `retry()` and handling of the `parked` status.** To run work again after a run ended without an answer, call `session.continue()` or submit it again.
6. **Update your `onReport` callback** if you pass one to `Harness.open`. It now takes one report tagged by `kind`, with the error on it. `session_failed` is now `storage_failed`, and a task the restart limit ends is reported as `task_interrupted` instead of `task_parked`.

### Minor Changes

- [#2796](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/pull/2796) [`edf1b52`](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/commit/edf1b5274b845571853a73fc1e8edd0ca4b62423) Thanks [@ben-reitz](https://github.com/ben-reitz)! - Support Pi 1.5 (`~1.5.0`; Pi 1.4 is no longer supported): `session.watch()` replaces `session.events()` and returns Pi's conversation view, `session.entries()` pages the transcript, `retry()` and the `parked` pending status are removed as Pi now ends crash-looping tasks, `submit()` takes `whenIdle: "reject"`, and the Pi tools build their schemas with `@earendil-works/pi-schema`, a new optional peer, as pi-ai no longer exports TypeBox's `Type`. See [pi-durable 1.5.0's changelog](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v1.5.0/packages/durable/CHANGELOG.md#150---2026-11-02).

- [#2797](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/pull/2797) [`77138fa`](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/commit/77138fa1a36f2c16f74c584ab3388058d5909182) Thanks [@ben-reitz](https://github.com/ben-reitz)! - Two new controls for the Pi harness, from Pi 1.5:

  - `continue()` starts a run without sending a new message. Use it to try again after a run ended without an answer, for example because the model errored or the run hit its turn limit.
  - `defaults.maxTurns` limits how many tool rounds a run can take. A run that reaches it ends without an answer, with reason `turn_limit`.

  See [Pi harness](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/harnesses/pi/).

### Patch Changes

- [#2795](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/pull/2795) [`3e21ee4`](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/commit/3e21ee48df129513310b844b05928bf3b5123d00) Thanks [@ben-reitz](https://github.com/ben-reitz)! - Add `Browser.functionDocs()`, `BrowserSession.functions`, report `notices`, opt-in scope locks (`browser.session({ lock: true })`, `session.lock()`) and `conversationScope()` to `agents/browser`, so code outside `browserTool` can run the same `browser` object. See [Browse the Web](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/tools/browser/).

- [#2795](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/pull/2795) [`3e21ee4`](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/commit/3e21ee48df129513310b844b05928bf3b5123d00) Thanks [@ben-reitz](https://github.com/ben-reitz)! - `browserTool` stops when the harness aborts its call, for pi, the AI SDK and TanStack AI. See [Browse the Web](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/tools/browser/).

- [#2798](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/pull/2798) [`62ccd87`](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/commit/62ccd8735b655dbe2d8d4f05716b6e6679958c8b) Thanks [@ben-reitz](https://github.com/ben-reitz)! - Pi models on the chat-completions wire (Workers AI, and OpenAI-compatible models through AI Gateway) now parse streamed tool-call arguments with pi-ai's own parser. When a model sends arguments that aren't valid JSON, the tool call now fails with an error the model can see and fix, instead of running with whatever arguments could be salvaged.

  See [Models for pi-ai](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/models/pi-ai/).

- [#2801](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/pull/2801) [`748e693`](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/commit/748e69393c034ceedfd718f9c14ab8346222335d) Thanks [@ben-reitz](https://github.com/ben-reitz)! - The pi `browserTool` gives code mode scripts the run as an object, with screenshots as image blocks for `image()`. See [Request cancellation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/agent-class/communication-channels/chat/chat-agents/#request-cancellation).

See [TanStack AI](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/packages/codemode/README.md#tanstack-ai).

## 0.31.0

This release adds internal hostnames to the browser. Give a Browser Run browser hostnames such as `preview.internal`, and its requests to them go to your agent instead of the internet, so the model can open a dev server, a workspace folder or another Worker in the same browser it uses for the web.

### Highlights

- **Internal hostnames:** pass up to 8 hostnames to `browserRun()` as `internalHosts`. Serve each one from a `fetch` function on your agent or from another Worker. See [Internal hostnames](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/browse-the-web.md#internal-hostnames).
- **Hosts the model points:** give a host a `target` schema, and the model chooses what it serves with `browser.assignHost()`, such as a container port or a folder in its workspace. Without a target, a host always serves the same thing.
- **Lighter installs without MCP servers:** `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and `@modelcontextprotocol/server` are now optional peer dependencies, so apps that don't serve MCP no longer install them.
- **Stable models:** `agents/models/ai-sdk` and `agents/models/pi-ai` are no longer experimental. See [Models](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/models.md).
- **Other changes:** `createMcpHandler` passes the verified token from `@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider` 1.x to tool callbacks as `context.http.authInfo`. `createAI` from `agents/models/pi-ai` sends pi-ai's Anthropic betas for catalog Claude models. `PiWhenBusy` accepts `"reject"`.
- **`browserTool` improvements:** the model's code runs in its own Dynamic Worker instead of on codemode, and is stopped from outside that Worker if it overruns its timeout. It can no longer close the browser or create a Live View link. `this.browser.session()` lets your own code drive the same browser. `createBrowserTools`, `createBrowserRuntime`, `BrowserConnector` and the Quick Action helpers are deprecated in favour of `browserTool`.

### Upgrading

You only need to make changes if you serve MCP or use `browserTool`.

If you serve MCP or use `agents/x402` or `agents/experimental/webmcp`:

1. **Add the MCP packages to your `package.json`** at the versions this release expects, since your package manager no longer installs them. Until you do, builds fail with an unresolved import.

   - `agents/mcp` (`McpAgent`, `WorkerTransport`, `createLegacyMcpHandler`) and `agents/x402`: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.32.1` and `@modelcontextprotocol/server@2.3.1`
   - `agents/mcp/server` (`createMcpHandler`): `@modelcontextprotocol/server@2.3.1`
   - `agents/experimental/webmcp`: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.32.1`

   See [Upgrading an existing `McpAgent` server](https://github.com/cloudflare/agents/blob/main/docs/agents/mcp-servers.md#upgrading-an-existing-mcpagent-server).

input.prompt: Summarise this migration guide precisely: the steps to move an McpAgent (SDK v1, Durable Object per session) server to createMcpHandler with SDK v2; what McpAgent features have no equivalent (per-session state, hibernation, alarms, SSE, server-to-client requests, session ids); how 2025-era clients are handled; any statement about McpAgent removal timeline; and any mention of the workers-oauth-provider version required. Quote exact phrases where possible.

result.output:
## McpAgent to createMcpHandler with SDK v2

**Migration paths**

- **Direct:** If the server doesn't depend on MCP session state, RPC, server-to-client requests, standalone streams, or event replay, move its tools into an SDK v2 factory and serve them with `createMcpHandler`.
- **Staged:** If it does, keep the McpAgent route, build stateless equivalents, serve both lanes, then drain the legacy lane.

**Steps**

1. Install `@modelcontextprotocol/server@2.3.1` and `zod`, pinning the version exactly.
2. Import `McpServer` from `@modelcontextprotocol/server` and move construction and tool registration into a factory function.
3. In the Worker's `fetch()`, call `createMcpHandler(factory)(request, env, ctx)`. Keep the object default export. Don't default-export the handler itself, because "Do not simplify this to `export default createMcpHandler(createServer)`." Wrangler would treat it as a `WorkerEntrypoint` class.
4. Remove SDK v1 transport and session options.
5. For the staged path, use `isLegacyRequest()` to route. Set `legacy: "reject"` on the stateless handler and point legacy requests at `MyMcpAgent.serve("/mcp")`.
6. Remove the legacy route and its protocol-only Durable Object binding only after clients stop depending on them. Treat the Durable Object migration as a separate deployment step.

**Features without a one-to-one equivalent**

The guide offers alternatives rather than direct mappings:

- **Per-session state:** Store data behind an explicit boundary (Durable Object, D1, KV, or R2), addressed by an authenticated, server-issued handle rather than a session ID.
- **Multi-step interaction state:** Use integrity-protected `requestState` with `input_required`, bound to the user, the original method and parameters, and an expiry.
- **Server-to-client requests (elicitation, sampling, roots):** Return `inputRequired(...)`. The client fulfils the requests and retries the operation.
- **Standalone list-change streams:** Use `subscriptions/listen`.
- **Session replay and transport recovery:** Make each request independently recoverable and persist progress in application storage.
- **Agent-to-McpAgent RPC:** Connect over Streamable HTTP by URL. The guide notes there is "no RPC transport for stateless servers."
- **Session IDs and session deletion:** The stateless path has no protocol session. The legacy fallback returns `405` for GET and DELETE, and no session ID persists.
- **SSE:** Standalone streams are unavailable in the fallback. `subscriptions/listen` uses an SSE response on the stateless path.
- **Hibernation and alarms:** The guide doesn't provide an equivalent for alarms. It mentions hibernation only in the context of rejected interactive calls and OAuth testing.

**Legacy clients**

- The default `legacy: "stateless"` mode supports ordinary tools, resources, and prompts. "Each POST receives a new server and transport."
- Limits include no standalone streams, no event replay, no session deletion, and pushed sampling, elicitation, and roots requests fail immediately.
- Use `legacy: "reject"` for stateless-only endpoints.
- Clients that need stateful features stay on the McpAgent lane until they migrate.
- On the client side, Agents falls back to `initialize` for legacy servers. Session IDs stored before v0.20.0 are discarded and the client reconnects.
- The guide doesn't use the term "2025-era."

**McpAgent removal timeline**

McpAgent is "deprecated and feature-frozen." The guide says "Migrate at your earliest convenience. No removal version is announced." Separately, the SDK v1 overload of `createMcpHandler` and `experimental_createMcpHandler` are "scheduled for removal in the next major version," but those are not McpAgent.

**workers-oauth-provider**

The guide doesn't mention `workers-oauth-provider` or any version of it. It covers only custom `AgentMcpOAuthProvider` implementations and OAuth types from `@modelcontextprotocol/client`.

---
name: mcp-2026-07-28-plan
description: 2026-11-09 assessment of moving ctxlayer off deprecated McpAgent (SDK v1) to agents createMcpHandler + SDK v2 for MCP protocol 2026-07-28 (server/discover). Verdict: NOT NOW; triggers + prep steps inside.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Facts (2026-11-09):** MCP `2026-07-28` is a released spec revision: stateless (no `initialize`, no `Mcp-Session-Id`, no GET SSE, no resumability), `server/discover` mandatory, elicitation via MRTR `input_required`, tasks moved to an extension, `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` on list results. Anthropic hosted clients already probe `server/discover` w/ `2026-07-28` and fall back to `initialize` on our 400.

**Stack gap:** ctxlayer = `agents@0.20.1` + `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.30` + `workers-oauth-provider@0.10.3`; `McpSessionDO extends McpAgent`. `McpAgent` is **deprecated + feature-frozen since agents 0.20.0** ("no removal version announced"), SDK v1 inside it can never answer `server/discover`. The only path to 2026-07-28 = `createMcpHandler` from `agents/mcp/server` + `@modelcontextprotocol/server@2.4.0` (has `server/discover`, `SUPPORTED_MODERN_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS=['2026-07-28']`, `legacy:'stateless'` lane serves 2025-era clients per-POST with no session). agents latest 0.33.0; from 0.31 the MCP SDKs are optional peers that must be pinned in package.json. oauth-provider 1.x (1.2.4) binds tokens to a resource and exposes `ctx.auth`; agents only reads it from 1.x.

**Why it's a redesign, not a swap (per-session state we rely on):** usage outbox in DO SQLite + alarm drain; hint-ledger once-per-session in DO SQLite; proxy registry built per session at init (bearer bound at init → `reload_upstreams`); A6/A7 per-request checks; `/sse` legacy endpoint (createMcpHandler serves no SSE). Stateless would also REMOVE known pain: serial-DO bottleneck (Driver 2–3 min calls), stale-session bearer gotcha, blockConcurrencyWhile resets, the 10–15 s WS-bridge wallTime tail.

**Verdict:** park. Fallback works, no client has dropped it, no public reports of clients requiring 2026-07-28. **Triggers to revisit:** a Claude client stops falling back / logs show `server/discover` 400 followed by no `initialize`; agents announces McpAgent removal; need for stateless benefits (serial DO) becomes acute. **Cheap prep worth doing anytime:** bump agents 0.20→0.33 keeping McpAgent (pin `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.32.2` explicitly), and plan oauth-provider 0.10→1.x separately (resource binding; 1.2.4 fixed `/sse`-resource refresh `invalid_target`). Staged migration pattern exists: `isLegacyRequest()` routes legacy → McpAgent, modern → stateless handler, drain later.

**Verdict: not worth it now.** The `server/discover` 400 isn't a bug to patch, it's the ceiling of the stack we're on, and getting past it means a stateless redesign of the session layer. Park it, with triggers.

**What's actually going on**

| Fact | Source |
|---|---|
| MCP `2026-07-28` is a released spec revision, not a draft | spec repo lists it beside 2025-11-25; "draft" is separate |
| It's a different protocol shape: no `initialize`, no sessions / `Mcp-Session-Id`, no GET SSE stream, no resumability; `server/discover` is mandatory; elicitation becomes "return `input_required`, client retries" | spec changelog |
| Anthropic's hosted clients already probe it, then fall back to `initialize` on our 400 | your logs this morning |
| Our stack: `agents@0.20.1` + MCP SDK `1.30` + `workers-oauth-provider@0.10.3`; `McpSessionDO extends McpAgent` | package.json |
| `McpAgent` is **deprecated and feature-frozen since agents 0.20.0** — the exact version we're on. "No removal version is announced." SDK v1 inside it will never answer `server/discover` | agents changelog + migration guide |
| The only path forward is `createMcpHandler` (`agents/mcp/server`) with SDK v2 (`@modelcontextprotocol/server@2.4.0`). That does implement `server/discover` and advertises `2026-07-28`, and its `legacy: "stateless"` lane keeps serving today's clients, but *per POST, with no session* | SDK 2.4.0 source |
| agents is now at 0.33.0; from 0.31 the MCP SDKs are optional peers you must pin yourself | changelog |
| oauth-provider 1.x (now 1.2.4) binds every token to a resource and exposes `ctx.auth`; agents only reads that from 1.x | changelog |

**Why it's a redesign for us.** Everything that makes ctxlayer more than a tool proxy lives in per-session Durable Object state, and the stateless handler has none:

| We rely on | Stateless equivalent |
|---|---|
| Proxy registry built once per session at `init` (catalogue, bearer bound at connect, `reload_upstreams`) | rebuild per request from D1/cache, or keep a per-*user* DO behind the handler |
| Usage outbox in DO SQLite + alarm drain | queue directly / per-user DO |
| First-result hint ledger "once per session" | key on user+day in D1/KV |
| `/sse` legacy endpoint | gone; `createMcpHandler` serves no SSE |
| Async `poll_task` / `list_tasks` | survives (D1-backed), but tasks moved to an extension in the new protocol |

Cloudflare's guide does describe a **staged** path: route with `isLegacyRequest()`, modern clients → stateless handler, legacy → `McpAgent`, drain later. That's the shape I'd use if we do it.

**What we'd gain** isn't nothing: the serial-DO bottleneck (Driver's 2–3 min calls blocking a session), the stale-session bearer gotcha, the `blockConcurrencyWhile` resets, and the 10–15 s WebSocket-bridge tail all disappear with a stateless handler. Those are real, but none is hurting today.

**Recommendation**
1. **Park the protocol move.** Revisit when one of these fires: logs show `server/discover` → 400 *not* followed by `initialize` (a client dropped the fallback); agents announces an `McpAgent` removal version; or the serial-DO pain becomes acute.
2. **Cheap prep, do anytime:** bump agents 0.20 → 0.33 while staying on `McpAgent` (pin `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.32.2` explicitly, as 0.31+ requires). Low risk, keeps us off a 13-minor-version cliff.
3. **Separate project, needed before any move:** oauth-provider 0.10 → 1.x. Resource-bound tokens; its 1.2.4 fix for `/sse`-bound grants refreshing with `invalid_target` is exactly the kind of trap we'd hit.

| checklist from the official migration guide (`resolveExternalToken`, `revokeExistingGrantsBatchSize`, `resourceMatchOriginOnly`, implicit/plain PKCE, `:` in user ids, TTL < 60 s) | none of it applies to us |

No version was pinned deliberately. `"agents": "^0.20.1"` was a caret range, and the only fixed point is that the MCP SDK has to match `agents` exactly. We also don't patch or override any library behaviour: the session class fills in the two hooks the library requires and adds one alarm handler. Every library internal our code depends on behaves the same in 0.33.

**How we got to 0.20.1** (from git history):

| Commit | Bump | Reason given |
|---|---|---|
| `9e95247` (2026-05-24) | added `agents` | initial MCP server; whatever version was current then |
| `ef59e60` (2026-06-26) | 0.13.2 → 0.16.2 | a fix in 0.16.0 (cloudflare/agents#1745) so an interrupted session teardown can no longer half-delete a session object |
| `7566070` (2026-08-11) | 0.16 → 0.20.1 | part of a toolchain upgrade; 0.20.1 was simply the latest release then. The SDK went to 1.30 because that was the version 0.20.1 required |

There are no `overrides`, `resolutions`, patch files or vendored copies in the repo.

**What our `McpSessionDO` adds on top of `McpAgent`:**

| Member | What it is | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | the library requires us to provide it | none |
| `init()` | the library's own extension point | none |
| `flushUsageOutbox()` | a new method the scheduler calls by name | none |
| `docMarkdown`, `stageUsage`, `upstreamProxy` | private helpers | none |

The library members we use are `this.env`, `this.props`, `this.ctx.storage.sql`, `this.schedule`, `this.getSessionId()` and `this.name`. No other file imports from `agents`.

**Library internals we depend on, checked against the 0.33 source:**

1. **We replace `this.server` inside `init()`.** That only works if the library reads `server` after `init()` returns. In both 0.20.1 and 0.33.0, `onStart()` runs `await this.init()` first and only then takes `this.server` and connects it, so behaviour is unchanged.
2. **`getSessionId()` parses `this.name`.** The code is the same in both versions. 0.22 changed where the object's name comes from, with a fallback for existing objects. Integration tests cover this path and pass.
3. **Pending usage drains scheduled under 0.20.** 0.20 kept them in a table called `cf_agents_schedules`. In 0.33, on first start each session moves those rows into its new job queue and drops the old table, so a drain scheduled just before the deploy still runs afterwards.
4. **Our own tables in the session object's storage** (`usage_outbox`, `hinted_upstreams`). All of the library's tables start with `cf_agent`, so the names can't clash.

The remaining risk is runtime-only, and the post-deploy check already covers it: confirm usage rows keep arriving after the yukitools release.
